entries.title: AI Exposure and the Changing Responsibilities in Job Postings
entries.summary: This preprint analyzes 50,000 job advertisements from 33 firms, finding that growing AI mentions often describe qualifications or company context rather than actual responsibilities. Human-annotation validation and checks on posting templates make its measurement approach worth examining, although advertised duties cannot establish actual task displacement.
entries.why_it_matters: When using job postings to plan skills investments, distinguish AI-related responsibilities from generic AI language and normalize for changes in posting length and templates. Otherwise, apparent changes in task demand may reflect rewritten advertisements rather than redesigned jobs.

entries.title: Effects of writing-based interventions on self-compassion and job burnout among psychotherapists: a three-arm randomized controlled trial and mediation analysis
entries.summary: A randomized trial of 67 psychotherapists compared six weeks of self-compassion-oriented writing, free writing, and a control condition, with both writing groups reporting greater reductions in emotional exhaustion than controls. The direct comparison and one-month follow-up are useful, but the small, non-preregistered study lacked an attention-matched control and found limited immediate superiority of structured over free writing.
entries.why_it_matters: For a psychotherapy workforce considering a voluntary writing-based support pilot, compare structured prompts with simpler free writing rather than assuming the specialized format adds value. Measure exhaustion and cynicism separately at baseline, completion, and follow-up before deciding whether to expand the program.

entries.title: Autism and personality testing: Improving reactions and mitigating adverse impact risk in hiring contexts
entries.source: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology
entries.summary: Comparing general and work-contextualized personality tests under applicant-like conditions, the study found that contextualization improved reactions but widened autistic–non-autistic score gaps and showed measurement bias. Testing both reactions and measurement invariance makes this useful for assessment design, although it does not establish effects on actual hiring outcomes.
entries.why_it_matters: Before replacing a general personality assessment with work-specific wording, evaluate subgroup score differences and measurement invariance alongside applicant reactions. Better acceptance of a test should not be treated as evidence of more equitable measurement.

entries.title: Age bias in resume screening: are HR professionals more biased than ChatGPT?
entries.summary: Two studies compared 800 HR professionals with 3,200 ChatGPT evaluations across younger and older applicants: the model penalized older applicants under both qualification conditions, while professionals did so when qualifications were ambiguous. The human–AI comparison and qualification contrast offer useful audit scenarios, but resume ratings do not establish real-world hiring effects or generalize automatically to other models.
entries.why_it_matters: When auditing resume screening, test age differences separately for clearly qualified and borderline applicants, including intersections with gender and job type. Compare human and automated evaluations rather than assuming either provides an unbiased benchmark.

entries.title: Meta-analysis with JASP, Part I: Classical approaches
entries.summary: This tutorial demonstrates graphical workflows for meta-analysis through three worked datasets, including multilevel and multivariate models with cluster-robust standard errors. Its concrete treatment of dependent effect sizes makes it worth opening for evidence synthesis, rather than as new evidence about any particular workforce intervention.
entries.why_it_matters: When pooling training, selection, or wellbeing evaluations that report multiple outcomes from the same participants, model the dependence instead of treating every effect as independent. The worked examples provide an accessible route to examining heterogeneity and reporting prediction intervals.

entries.title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
entries.summary: This preprint repeats controlled founder-evaluation audits over 13 months, using 248,400 API calls, and finds that bias patterns changed even under an unchanged model identifier. Identical prompts, name-clustered inference, and a shorter-interval replication strengthen the comparison, but the task concerns investment rather than hiring and cannot identify the mechanism behind serving changes.
entries.why_it_matters: For LLM-assisted people decisions, retain a fixed audit set and rerun it periodically and after model replacements instead of treating an unchanged identifier as proof that earlier fairness results remain valid. Record the model identifier, collection date, prompts, and outputs so comparisons remain interpretable.

entries.title: Task reflexivity as a pathway linking task interdependence and knowledge sharing
entries.source: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology
entries.summary: A daily diary study of 156 South Korean construction workers, providing 1,404 observations, linked daily task interdependence with task reflection and knowledge sharing. Within-person analyses distinguish day-to-day fluctuations from stable employee differences, although the observational design does not establish that increasing reflection causes sharing.
entries.why_it_matters: When investigating coordination problems in interdependent work, measure daily task demands, reflection, and knowledge sharing rather than relying only on a one-time engagement survey. Use the findings to motivate a controlled pilot of brief task reviews, not to justify a company-wide intervention without testing.

entries.title: A technical framework for HR-driven imbalanced classification: pipeline architecture, oversampling algorithms, ablation analysis, and threshold engineering for data scientist job-change prediction
entries.summary: Using 19,158 records, the study compared 90 model–sampling configurations and directly demonstrated that oversampling before cross-validation inflated AUC enough to reverse model rankings. Feature ablations strengthen its engineering lessons, but the outcome is self-reported job-change propensity, not verified turnover.
entries.why_it_matters: When building retention-risk models, keep oversampling inside training folds and compare against an unresampled baseline before accepting apparent improvements. Evaluate decision thresholds separately rather than treating a model trained on intentions as a validated predictor of actual departures.

entries.title: A Taxonomy-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Retrieval Effectiveness and Fairness Evaluation in Hiring
entries.summary: This preprint benchmarks candidate retrieval using multilingual synthetic profiles, demographic counterfactual twins, and comparisons with real historical interactions. General-purpose embedding rankings did not reliably predict hiring-task performance; applicability is limited by synthetic relevance labels, small-scale human validation, and coverage concentrated in European languages and technology roles.
entries.why_it_matters: When selecting a model for multilingual talent search, test job-specific ranking quality alongside gender-perturbation sensitivity in each deployment language. Use the benchmark as an initial diagnostic, then validate shortlisted models on representative local profiles rather than choosing from general leaderboard scores alone.

entries.title: Rethinking how employee innovation is enabled at work: a process analysis of HR bundles and innovative work behaviors
entries.source: Journal of Organizational Effectiveness: People and Performance
entries.summary: A three-firm consulting case study combined 34 interviews across hierarchical levels with organizational documents to examine how innovation opportunities evolve. It identifies reciprocal patterns in which demonstrated innovation changes employees’ subsequent discretion, offering a contextual explanation rather than a causal estimate of HR-practice effectiveness.
entries.why_it_matters: When comparing innovation ratings across career stages, measure permission and opportunity to innovate alongside idea generation and implementation. In consulting work, investigate whether low observed innovation reflects restricted discretion before interpreting it as an individual capability deficit.

entries.title: Job resources and thriving sequentially explain the effects of on- and off-the-job embeddedness on performance
entries.summary: Three-wave data from 340 employees and 111 supervisors in India linked workplace and community embeddedness with resources, thriving, and supervisor-rated performance. Multiple sources strengthen the evidence beyond a single employee questionnaire, but both proposed mediators were measured together, leaving their sequence and causality unresolved.
entries.why_it_matters: When investigating why well-connected employees perform better, distinguish workplace embeddedness from community ties and add autonomy, collaboration, development opportunities, learning, and vitality to the measurement plan. Measure these repeatedly before using mediation results to justify a particular intervention.

entries.title: Does AI Reinforce Gender Stereotypes? Gender Bias in Job Descriptions Generated by 40+ Large Language Models
entries.summary: An audit of 48 language models compared 4,608 job descriptions generated from matched gender-neutral and gender-coded titles. Some measured differences persisted despite prompt changes; salary differences were not robust across all analyses, and applicant outcomes were not measured.
entries.why_it_matters: When using AI to draft vacancies, start with gender-neutral job titles and audit the resulting language and salary suggestions rather than relying on prompt corrections alone.

entries.title: When Does Workload Undermine Innovative Behavior? The Joint Moderating Roles of Empowering Leadership and Perceived Organizational Support
entries.summary: Across three waves of data from 349 employees and 30 supervisors at one Chinese firm, workload was associated with greater exhaustion and lower innovative behavior. The observational design does not establish that workload caused either outcome.
entries.why_it_matters: When investigating a decline in innovation, analyze workload and exhaustion alongside employees’ perceptions of managerial and organizational support rather than treating innovation scores in isolation.

entries.title: Between support and effort: how managerial need support and employee need crafting longitudinally associate with employee basic psychological needs
entries.summary: In a three-wave study of US and UK employees, managerial support and employees’ own job-crafting behaviors had different associations with autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Of 796 initial participants, 500 completed the final wave; the associations do not establish causation.
entries.why_it_matters: In an employee-listening program, measure autonomy, competence, and connection separately, alongside manager support and employees’ opportunities to shape their work, rather than relying on a single needs score.

entries.title: When AI thinks about culture: comparing language-based and empirical measures of individualism–collectivism
entries.summary: Researchers compared five language models’ country-level cultural estimates with a survey-based index covering 102 countries and territories. Despite strong overall alignment, the models systematically overstated Western individualism and understated it in Confucian East Asian societies relative to the benchmark.
entries.why_it_matters: Before using AI-generated cultural profiles to design a multinational employee survey or management program, compare them with current, context-specific evidence and avoid treating national averages as individual traits.

entries.title: Triggers of job insecurity: a latent transition approach to understanding how people construe threats to their jobs
entries.summary: Using worker surveys and latent profile and transition analyses, the researchers found that specific combinations of perceived threats were associated with greater job insecurity than diffuse uncertainty. Profiles also changed over time.
entries.why_it_matters: Employee surveys could distinguish concerns about personal job prospects, organizational changes and wider economic threats rather than relying on a single insecurity score. Repeated measurement may help teams see how concerns change during restructuring.

entries.title: Confidence intervals for the difference between proportions after multiple imputation: a simulation study comparing different strategies
entries.summary: Simulations compared three confidence-interval methods for differences between proportions after multiple imputation. Wald intervals had inadequate coverage in small samples with extreme proportions, while Agresti-Caffo and Newcombe-Wilson methods performed better.
entries.why_it_matters: Analysts comparing promotion or attrition rates with missing data can consider alternatives to Wald intervals, especially for small groups or rare outcomes. The findings apply to the missing-data scenarios tested, not every imputation setting.

entries.title: The power of perception: the impact of inclusivity policies and diversity climate on employee well-being
entries.source: Equality, Diversity and Inclusion: An International Journal
entries.summary: A survey of 361 faculty and staff at a southeastern US university examined perceptions of inclusion policies, diversity climate and well-being. Favorable policy perceptions and diversity climate were associated with better reported outcomes, including job satisfaction and turnover intentions.
entries.why_it_matters: An inclusion assessment could measure employees’ experiences of policies and workplace climate alongside whether policies exist. The single-university survey cannot establish that policy perceptions caused the outcomes.

entries.title: Who Perceives Work Performance Improvements from Generative AI Use in Government, Early-Stage Diffusion? Exploring the Roles of Organizational Power and Motivation on Work Performance
entries.summary: In survey responses from 1,608 Korean civil servants, more frequent generative AI use and intrinsic motivation were associated with greater perceived performance benefits. The outcome was self-reported improvement, not independently measured productivity.
entries.why_it_matters: AI rollout evaluations can compare perceived benefits across usage and motivation levels while collecting separate evidence of work quality and productivity. The associations alone do not show that greater use causes better performance.

entries.title: The Coordination of Both Volunteers and Paid Staff in Nonprofit Organizations: A Scoping Review and Future Research Agenda
entries.summary: A scoping review of 23 articles organized research on volunteer–staff coordination around organizational design, identity and culture, and relationships and communication. It found that structural and relational approaches are often studied separately.
entries.why_it_matters: Nonprofit workforce assessments can examine role boundaries and reporting structures alongside communication between volunteers and paid staff. The review identifies ways to frame an assessment rather than proving that a particular coordination practice works.

entries.title: Development and validation of a measure of work decision styles
entries.summary: Four studies developed a 20-item measure of analytical, intuitive, collaborative, and decisive work decision styles. Validation included factor analysis, item response theory, and associations with self-reported job performance.
entries.why_it_matters: The measure could support research into decision-making and development needs at work. Its relationship with performance needs further testing against outcomes beyond self-reports.

entries.title: Work engagement and mental well-being in the ICT age: investigating the role of job resources among white-collar workers in Europe
entries.summary: An analysis of 20,347 white-collar workers across 36 countries found that opportunities to demonstrate competence were strongly associated with engagement, while trust and cooperation were important predictors of mental well-being.
entries.why_it_matters: Employee surveys and work-design reviews could measure opportunities to use skills and team cooperation alongside technology use. The observational findings do not establish that changing those resources will improve outcomes.

entries.title: Workplace AI Trust: Scale Development, Preliminary Psychometric Validation, and Associations with Employee AI Experience
entries.summary: Researchers developed an eight-item workplace AI trust scale using a survey of Polish working adults. The items showed internal consistency, but model fit and evidence for comparisons between groups were mixed.
entries.why_it_matters: The scale offers candidate questions for research into employee AI experience. Practitioners should validate it locally before comparing groups or using scores to guide consequential decisions.

entries.title: Conservation in place: perceived pay inequity as a chronic occupational stressor in a high-unemployment labor market
entries.summary: A secondary analysis of interviews with ten employees and managers at one South African consumer-goods organization examined responses to perceived pay unfairness. Some participants described remaining in their jobs while reducing discretionary effort.
entries.why_it_matters: The findings suggest pairing retention metrics with confidential measures of perceived pay fairness and employee voice. The small, single-organization study cannot estimate how widespread these responses are.

entries.title: Exploring the ambivalence of job autonomy in agile work context: A qualitative study
entries.summary: Interviews with 20 employees in one agile organization found that participants valued autonomy but also described constraints and demands associated with self-organization and responsibility.
entries.why_it_matters: Work-design assessments could distinguish advertised autonomy from employees’ experienced discretion, support, and workload. The interviews provide context for survey design rather than evidence of effects across organizations.

entries.title: Role uncertainty in AI-enabled organizational change: linking perceived AI adoption to job stress
entries.summary: A three-wave survey of 355 employees in Japanese organizations found that perceived AI adoption was associated with greater role ambiguity and subsequent job stress. The association between adoption and ambiguity was weaker where change communication was rated more highly.
entries.why_it_matters: When evaluating an AI rollout, measure role clarity and change communication alongside stress. The observational design does not establish that communication caused the difference.

entries.title: How Safety Incident Reporting Decisions Are Made: A Multilevel, Process-Oriented Perspective
entries.summary: Interviews with 34 shipbuilding and ship-repair employees examined how they decide whether to report safety incidents. Reasons for reporting and not reporting were not simply opposites, and workers described interacting personal, organizational and economic considerations.
entries.why_it_matters: Incident counts alone can miss reporting barriers. Safety teams could supplement them with confidential interviews about the effort, perceived consequences and practical constraints involved in reporting.

entries.title: Mental distress diverges by gender across the transition to first parenthood and is not consistently buffered by working from home
entries.summary: A UK household-panel event study found differing distress trajectories for employed women and men after first parenthood, but no consistent evidence that working from home beforehand buffered those trajectories. Results for mothers were affected by selection into continued employment, and remote-work estimates were imprecise.
entries.why_it_matters: When assessing support for new parents, track well-being and employment exits rather than assuming remote work is sufficient. Interpret gender comparisons cautiously when leave and workforce exits affect who remains observable.

entries.title: Associations between digital and automated work and psychosocial outcomes: Cross-sectional results from the Gutenberg Health Study
entries.source: International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health
entries.summary: In a cross-sectional German study of 5,730 participants, digital work had mixed associations with job satisfaction, engagement and intentions to leave, while automated work was associated with higher burnout and lower satisfaction. Technical and skill-related demands were also associated with several adverse outcomes.
entries.why_it_matters: Workforce surveys can distinguish digital work, automation, technology-related demands and employees’ experiences instead of treating technology exposure as one measure. The associations do not establish that technology caused the outcomes.

entries.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
entries.summary: This preprint models how choosing between independent work and AI answers could affect skill acquisition and retention over repeated tasks. Under its assumptions, incentives for independent practice can help sustain skill even when AI-assisted task accuracy remains high.
entries.why_it_matters: The model can inform decisions about protected practice time and how to measure skill retention during AI deployment. Its predictions need empirical testing before being treated as evidence of workplace effects.

entries.title: Uncovering the Mechanisms of Policy Interventions: A Difference-In-Differences Framework for Mediation Analysis
entries.summary: The authors develop a difference-in-differences framework for studying how HR interventions affect outcomes through intermediate mechanisms. The method accommodates some unobserved confounding but requires assumptions about untreated trends and changes over time.
entries.why_it_matters: People analytics teams evaluating a training rollout could use the framework to examine whether skill acquisition helps explain performance changes, while making the required causal assumptions explicit.

entries.title: The Organizational Benefits of Neurodiversity: A Strategic Human Capital–Based Systematic Review and Research Agenda
entries.summary: A systematic review of 88 studies examines how HR research has approached the organizational benefits of neurodiversity. It finds that evidence on organization-level outcomes remains limited and uneven.
entries.why_it_matters: Teams evaluating neuroinclusive hiring or workplace adjustments can use the review to plan measures of implementation and outcomes without assuming that organizational benefits are already established.

entries.title: Watched by the algorithm: algorithmic monitoring, worker resistance and well-being in the gig economy
entries.summary: A three-wave survey of 224 gig workers in Pakistan linked perceived algorithmic monitoring with worker resistance, while an experiment with 115 participants examined monitoring and fairness together. Resistance patterns in the experiment did not always match the researchers’ predictions.
entries.why_it_matters: Organizations assessing worker-monitoring systems could measure perceived fairness and resistance alongside well-being rather than relying on productivity indicators alone.

entries.title: The fluid emergence of GenAI roles in temporary teams: How teams calibrate delegation under shifting situational demands
entries.summary: Interviews with 28 teams during a 48-hour innovation sprint identified different roles that generative AI assumed as teams moved between tasks. Each role presented distinct opportunities and risks, including trivial advice and excessive reliance.
entries.why_it_matters: Managers designing AI-assisted teamwork can specify which tasks may be delegated, what output is expected, and who reviews it at each stage of a project.

entries.title: The new meaning of office: how hybrid work changes formal organizational structure from a place perspective
entries.summary: Across 49 interviews in two international organizations, researchers observed changes in how HR positions were grouped and centralized alongside shifts toward hybrid work. Employees also described the office as a place for social connection.
entries.why_it_matters: When reviewing a hybrid-work policy, people teams could track changes in reporting lines and collaboration alongside office attendance, rather than treating attendance as a sufficient measure of organizational impact.
